::: {.callout-tip}
#### Learning Objectives

- Know how to use `filterFeatures` to filter DIA-NN precursor data by Q-value thresholds
- Know how to use `joinAssays` to combine per-sample `SummarizedExperiment` objects into a single combined set
- Know how to identify and remove contaminant proteins
- Be able to explore and visualise missing values in DIA proteomics data
- Understand how to filter sparse precursors based on a missing value threshold
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup

knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = here::here("course_files/dia"))
```

```{r}
#| label: load-packages-and-data
#| include: false

library("QFeatures")
library("naniar")
library("tidyr")
library("dplyr")
library("ggplot2")
library("patchwork")

load("preprocessed/lesson02.rda", verbose = TRUE)
```

Now that we have our precursor-level data stored in a `QFeatures` object, the next step is to carry out data cleaning --- filtering to retain only high-confidence identifications and removing precursors with excessive missing values across samples.

## Filtering by Q-value

::: {.callout-discussion}
#### Discussion

Before reading on, consider the following:

- Why do we need to filter the DIA-NN output at all?
  What would happen if we kept all identifications?
- What do the Q-value columns represent, and what is the difference between run-level and library-level Q-values?
- What threshold would you choose?
- What impact could this filtering have on the downstream analysis and results?
:::

::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"}
DIA-NN reports identifications made with a range of confidence.
Without a filter, incorrect identifications enter the quantification, and proteins that are not in the sample can appear in the results.

A run-level Q-value describes the confidence in an identification within a single run.
A library-level Q-value describes the confidence across the whole experiment, calculated in the first pass of match-between-runs.

A threshold of 0.01 is the usual choice.
A stricter threshold removes more false identifications, but also more true ones.

The run-level filters are applied separately in each run, so a precursor that passes in some runs and fails in others becomes a missing value in the runs where it fails.
The library-level Q-values are the same in every run, so those filters remove a precursor from all runs at once.
Filtering therefore adds missing values as well as removing precursors.
:::

DIA-NN assigns a Q-value to each precursor and protein group identification.
Keeping the identifications with a Q-value at or below a threshold controls the false discovery rate (FDR) among everything retained: at 0.01, we expect 1% of the retained identifications to be incorrect.
The Q-value columns are described in the DIA-NN Q-value callout in lesson 01.

Our data was processed with match-between-runs (MBR) enabled.
DIA-NN then makes two passes over the data: the first builds an empirical spectral library from the runs, and the second reanalyses every run against that library.
The library-level Q-values (`Lib.Q.Value`, `Lib.PG.Q.Value`) are the global Q-values from the first pass, calculated against the full library.
They carry the experiment-wide confidence that `Global.Q.Value` and `Global.PG.Q.Value` carry in an analysis without MBR, so we filter on them together with the run-level Q-values (`Q.Value`, `PG.Q.Value`).
We apply a standard 1% FDR threshold (Q-value ≤ 0.01) to all four columns.

{{< include ../_shared/_filterFeatures.md >}}

Since we want to apply the Q-value filter across all per-sample `SummarizedExperiment`s simultaneously, we do not pass an `i` argument --- this causes `filterFeatures` to apply the filter to every set in the `QFeatures` object.

```{r}
#| label: filter-qvalues
dia_qf

dia_qf <- dia_qf %>%
  filterFeatures(~ Q.Value <= 0.01) %>% # Run-level precursor Q-value
  filterFeatures(~ PG.Q.Value <= 0.01) %>% # Run-level protein group Q-value
  filterFeatures(~ Lib.Q.Value <= 0.01) %>% # Library-level precursor Q-value
  filterFeatures(~ Lib.PG.Q.Value <= 0.01) # Library-level protein group Q-value

dia_qf
```

We can see how many precursors remain per sample after filtering by inspecting the number of rows in each per-sample set.

```{r}
#| label: histogram-precursors-after-qvalue-filter
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 4

hist(
  nrows(dia_qf),
  xlab = "Precursors",
  main = "Precursor counts per sample\nafter Q-value filtering"
)
```

## Joining per-sample sets into a single precursor set

After filtering, our `QFeatures` object contains one `SummarizedExperiment` per sample run.
To work with the data combined across all samples, we use the `joinAssays` function.
This merges all per-sample sets into a single combined set called `"precursors"`, aligning features (precursors) by their `Precursor.Id`.
Where a precursor was not detected in a particular sample, the corresponding entry will be `NA`.

```{r}
#| label: join-sets
dia_qf <- joinAssays(
  x = dia_qf,
  i = names(dia_qf),
  name = "precursors",
  fcol = "Precursor.Id"
)
```

Note that `joinAssays` only retains `rowData` columns that are shared across all sets and have consistent values --- run-specific metrics such as `Q.Value`, `PEP`, and `Run` are therefore dropped from the combined set.
This is expected: these per-run quality metrics were used for filtering in the previous step and are no longer needed.
We can confirm which columns are dropped by comparing the `rowData` names before and after joining.

```{r}
#| label: compare-rowdata-columns
# rowData columns in the per-sample sets
sample_level_rdata_names <- rowDataNames(dia_qf)[[1]]

# rowData columns in the combined set
joined_rdata_names <- rowDataNames(dia_qf)[["precursors"]]

# Columns present in sample-level sets but dropped from the combined set
setdiff(sample_level_rdata_names, joined_rdata_names)
```

::: {.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge: Comparing `rowData` before and after joining

{{< level 2 >}}

Compare the `rowData` of the first per-sample set with the `rowData` of the `"precursors"` set.
This code only inspects the object, so it does not change `dia_qf`.
Run it before the per-sample sets are removed in the next section.

1. How do the numbers of rows and columns differ between the two sets?
2. We filtered on `Q.Value`, `PG.Q.Value`, `Lib.Q.Value` and `Lib.PG.Q.Value`. Which of these four columns are still present in `"precursors"`?

Based on your results:

- Why does `"precursors"` have a different number of rows from a single per-sample set?
- Why are some of the four Q-value columns kept and others dropped?
- What does this mean for the order in which we filter and join?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>`rowData()` returns a `DataFrame` for a single set, so `dim()` gives its rows and columns.
`rowDataNames(dia_qf)[["precursors"]]` lists the column names of the combined set, and `%in%` tests whether a name is in that list.</details>

::::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"}
**Task 1**

```{r}
#| label: compare-rowdata-dims
dim(rowData(dia_qf[[1]]))
dim(rowData(dia_qf[["precursors"]]))
```

**Task 2**

```{r}
#| label: compare-rowdata-qvalues
filter_cols <- c("Q.Value", "PG.Q.Value", "Lib.Q.Value", "Lib.PG.Q.Value")
filter_cols %in% rowDataNames(dia_qf)[["precursors"]]
```

The `"precursors"` set contains every precursor detected in at least one sample, so it has more rows than any single per-sample set.
It has fewer columns because `joinAssays` keeps a `rowData` column only if every set has it and its values agree for the precursors the sets share.
`Q.Value` and `PG.Q.Value` take different values in different runs, so they are dropped.
`Lib.Q.Value` and `Lib.PG.Q.Value` have the same value in every run for a given precursor, so they are kept.
Filters on run-level Q-values can therefore only be applied to the per-sample sets, before joining.
:::::
:::

## Removing individual sample-level assays

Now that the per-sample data has been joined into the `"precursors"` set, we no longer need to keep the individual per-sample `SummarizedExperiment` objects.
To reduce the size of our QFeatures object, we identify the sets for individual samples and remove them.
This isn't strictly necessary for this dataset, but it may be if you have a very large experiment.
It also helps to keep the object tidy and focused on the combined set for downstream analysis.

The `sampleMap` is an internal table in a `QFeatures` object that records which samples are present in each assay.
We can inspect it before removing the per-sample sets --- at this point it contains one row per sample per assay, so with 31 samples, it has 62 rows - one row each for the original per-sample assay and for the `"precursors"` assay.

```{r}
#| label: show-samplemap
sampleMap(dia_qf)
```

After calling `removeAssay`, the 31 per-sample assays are dropped and their corresponding `sampleMap` entries are removed, leaving only the rows for `"precursors"`.
You will see a message indicating that sampleMap rows have been harmonised --- this is expected behaviour.

```{r}
#| label: remove-per-sample-sets
sets_to_rm <- which(names(dia_qf) != "precursors")
dia_qf <- removeAssay(dia_qf, i = sets_to_rm)

sampleMap(dia_qf)
```

## Removing contaminant proteins

In any proteomics experiment, some identified peptides will derive from contaminant proteins rather than the sample of biological interest.
Common contaminants include proteins introduced during sample preparation --- for example, human keratins from skin or hair, bovine serum albumin from cell culture media, and trypsin used for proteolytic digestion.
These proteins are not informative for the biological question and should be removed before downstream analysis.

It is standard practice to include a curated contaminants database alongside the primary sequence database during the database search.
For this data, we used a modified version of the contaminants fasta from [Hao Group's Protein Contaminant Libraries for DDA and DIA Proteomics](https://github.com/HaoGroup-ProtContLib/Protein-Contaminant-Libraries-for-DDA-and-DIA-Proteomics/) @Frankenfield2022, where we removed the contaminants from Fetal Bovine Serum, which are not relevant here.
The entries in this contaminant database are named with a `Cont_` prefix, which is carried through into the `Protein.Ids` column of the DIA-NN output, making them straightforward to identify computationally.

We can inspect the `rowData` to check the contaminants can be identified as expected.

```{r}
#| label: count-contaminants
# Extract the rowData
rd <- rowData(dia_qf[['precursors']]) %>%
  data.frame()

table(grepl('Cont_', rd$Protein.Ids))
```

We now remove precursors with a contaminant match from our data.

{{< include ../_shared/_copy_assay_rationale.md >}}

We create a copy of the `"precursors"` set called `"precursors_no_cont"`.
After filtering, this set will contain only precursors that do not originate from contaminants.
We use `plot` to visualise the assay structure before and after adding the link.

```{r}
#| label: add-no-contaminant-set
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 3

dia_qf <- addAssay(dia_qf, dia_qf[["precursors"]], name = "precursors_no_cont")

plot(dia_qf)

dia_qf <- addAssayLink(dia_qf, from = "precursors", to = "precursors_no_cont")

plot(dia_qf)
```

We then use `filterFeatures` to retain only precursors whose `Protein.Ids` field contains no `Cont_` entry.
We specify the `i` argument to apply the filter only to the `"precursors_no_cont"` set.
This retains the original `"precursors"` assay with all precursors for reference, while the new set contains only precursors from non-contaminant proteins.

```{r}
#| label: filter-contaminants
dia_qf <- filterFeatures(
  dia_qf,
  ~ !grepl("Cont_", Protein.Ids),
  i = "precursors_no_cont"
)

dia_qf
```

## Exploring missing values

DIA proteomics data can exhibit substantial missing values because proteins must be detected independently in each sample run.
Before filtering, it is important to understand the extent and distribution of missing values in the data.

We use the `nNA` function to calculate the proportion of missing values per precursor (row) and per sample (column).

```{r}
#| label: count-missing-values
precursors_missing <- nNA(dia_qf, i = "precursors_no_cont")

print(precursors_missing)
```

::: {.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge: Visualising missing values

{{< level 2 >}}

Using the `precursors_missing` object, create plots to explore the distribution of missing values in the data.

1. Plot a histogram for the proportion of missing values across *precursors*.
2. Plot the proportion of missing values per *sample*, coloured by *group*.

Based on your plots:

- Do most precursors have missing values?
- Are there any precursors or samples with an unusually high proportion of missing values?
- Does the proportion of missing values differ between groups?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>The `precursors_missing` object contains
two data frames: `nNArows` (one row per precursor) and `nNAcols` (one row
per sample), each with a `pNA` column giving the proportion of missing
values.</details>

::::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"}
**Task 1**

```{r}
#| label: histogram-missing-per-precursor
hist(
  precursors_missing$nNArows$pNA,
  xlab = "Proportion missing values",
  main = "Missing values per precursor"
)
```

**Task 2**

```{r}
#| label: barplot-missing-per-sample
precursors_missing$nNAcols %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  merge(data.frame(colData(dia_qf)), by.x = "name", by.y = "runCol") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = name, y = pNA, group = group, fill = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Sample", y = "Proportion missing values") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  theme_classic()
```
:::::
:::

### Patterns of missingness across samples

The plots above show *how many* values are missing per precursor and per sample, but not *which* samples share missing values.
An upset plot shows this.
Each sample is a set, and each bar counts the precursors missing in exactly that combination of samples.

```{r}
#| label: plot-missingness-upset
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-width: 10
#| warning: false

missing_data <- dia_qf[["precursors_no_cont"]] %>% assay() %>% data.frame()

# Passing the column names to sets keeps the samples in the order of the
# assay columns. Without it, samples are ordered by their number of missing
# values and keep.order has no effect.
naniar::gg_miss_upset(
  missing_data,
  sets = paste0(colnames(missing_data), "_NA"),
  keep.order = TRUE,
  nintersects = 50
)
```

When a few intersections dominate the plot, they tell us something about the data.
If the dominant combinations are the samples of one group, those precursors are likely low in abundance in that group, or absent from it.
If a single sample appears in many intersections, that sample may have a technical problem, such as lower loading or poorer chromatography.
In this dataset, the largest intersection is 83 precursors missing only in COVID_E5, which is the sample with the most missing values overall.
The next largest are precursors missing in one other sample, or detected in only one sample; the second kind are removed by the filter in the next section.
None of these is large compared with the 1,854 precursors that have at least one missing value, so no single pattern dominates.

### Why precursors go missing

A precursor is missing from a run when DIA-NN did not detect it in that run.
Low-intensity precursors are missed more often, because their signal is closer to the background.
There is no fixed intensity below which detection fails, though.
Precursors are also missed at high intensity, for example when their elution profile cannot be separated from that of another precursor, and often for reasons that are not easy to predict.

::: {.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge: Missing values and intensity

{{< level 2 >}}

For each precursor in the `"precursors_no_cont"` set, calculate the proportion of samples in which it is missing and the mean of its log2 intensity over the samples in which it was detected.
Plot one against the other.

- How does the proportion of missing values change with intensity?
- Are high-intensity precursors ever missing?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>Extract the matrix with `assay()`.
`rowMeans(is.na(x))` gives the proportion missing per row, and
`rowMeans(log2(x), na.rm = TRUE)` the mean of the observed log2
values.</details>

::::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"}
```{r}
#| label: plot-missingness-intensity
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 5
precursor_intensities <- assay(dia_qf[["precursors_no_cont"]])

precursor_detection <- data.frame(
  mean_log2 = rowMeans(log2(precursor_intensities), na.rm = TRUE),
  prop_missing = rowMeans(is.na(precursor_intensities))
)

ggplot(precursor_detection, aes(x = mean_log2, y = prop_missing)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x) +
  labs(
    x = "Mean log2 intensity (detected samples)",
    y = "Proportion of samples missing"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

The proportion of missing values falls steadily as intensity rises, with no single intensity at which it drops to zero.
Some high-intensity precursors are still missing from a few samples.

The intensities on the x-axis are only those of the samples in which a precursor was detected.
For a precursor that is often missing, these are its higher values, so its mean is an overestimate of its true average intensity, and the low end of the curve is steeper than the plot suggests.
:::::
:::

A useful way to describe this is the probability that a precursor is detected, as a function of its true intensity.
If this probability did not depend on intensity, values would go missing at random and could be ignored without losing information.
If every precursor below a certain intensity were missed and every one above it detected, the missing values would simply be a hard cut-off at that intensity.
Real data lies between these two extremes: the probability of detection rises steadily with intensity, without a sharp threshold [@Li2023].
The `limpa` package describes missingness in this way and estimates the curve from the data with `limpa::dpc()` [@Li2025].

Two things follow for the analysis:

- A missing value carries some information: the precursor was probably at low intensity in that run.
- A single missing value cannot tell us whether a precursor was present below detection or absent from the sample.

### How we handle missing values

In this course we do not replace missing values.
Filling them in with a substitute value and then analysing the data as if every value had been measured treats guesses as measurements, which distorts the variance estimates that the statistical tests depend on.
We will see an example of this in the statistical analysis lesson.

Instead, we handle missing values in three steps:

1. Remove precursors detected in too few samples to be quantified reliably (next section).
2. Summarise each protein from the precursors detected in each sample, using `robustSummary`, which works on the observed values only (next lesson).
3. Before testing, keep only proteins quantified in at least three samples of every group (statistical analysis lesson).

A consequence of step 3 is that a protein detected in one group and absent from another is never tested, even though that pattern can be the most interesting one in an experiment.
Proteins like these need a method that uses the missing values themselves as information.
`limpa` [@Li2025] is one such method: it uses the detection curve to estimate an abundance and a standard error for every protein in every sample (`limpa::dpcQuant()`), and carries that uncertainty into a `limma` analysis (`limpa::dpcDE()`).

## Filtering sparse precursors

Precursors that are missing across the majority of samples provide little useful quantitative information and may introduce noise into downstream analyses.
We filter out precursors with excessive missing values using the `filterNA` function, where the `pNA` argument specifies the maximum proportion of missing values allowed per precursor.

The choice of threshold involves a trade-off: stricter thresholds (lower `pNA`) remove more precursors and produce a cleaner but smaller dataset; more permissive thresholds retain more precursors but include those with very sparse quantification, which are more likely to be inaccurately quantified.
Here we use `pNA = 0.75`, meaning a precursor must be observed in at least 25% of samples --- with 31 samples, this corresponds to a minimum of approximately 8 observations.
Further filtering will be applied at the protein level in the statistical analysis, where we will require proteins to be quantified in at least 3 replicates per group before testing.

We create a copy called `"precursors_filtered_missing"` --- after filtering, this set will contain only precursors that meet the missing value threshold.

```{r}
#| label: add-filtered-missing-set
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 3

dia_qf <- addAssay(
  dia_qf,
  dia_qf[["precursors_no_cont"]],
  name = "precursors_filtered_missing"
)

dia_qf <- addAssayLink(
  dia_qf,
  from = "precursors_no_cont",
  to = "precursors_filtered_missing"
)
```

Now we perform the missing value filtering on the new assay, again specifying the `i` argument to apply the filter to only the desired set.

```{r}
#| label: filter-sparse-precursors
dia_qf <- dia_qf %>%
  filterNA(pNA = 0.75, i = "precursors_filtered_missing")

nrow(dia_qf[["precursors_no_cont"]])
nrow(dia_qf[["precursors_filtered_missing"]])
```

The filter retains `r nrow(dia_qf[["precursors_filtered_missing"]])` of the `r nrow(dia_qf[["precursors_no_cont"]])` non-contaminant precursors.

## Removing a sample

We keep all 31 samples, because none stood out in the checks in the previous lesson.
If a sample did need to be removed, for example after a failed injection, we would subset the `QFeatures` object by column, which removes the sample from every set at once.
Here `Ctr_A1` is only an example, and the chunk is not run.

```{r}
#| label: drop-sample-example
#| eval: false
dia_qf <- dia_qf[, dia_qf$runCol != "Ctr_A1"]
```

```{r}
#| label: save-lesson03
#| include: false

save(dia_qf, file = "preprocessed/lesson03.rda")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Key Points

- Filtering DIA-NN Q-value columns (`Q.Value`, `PG.Q.Value`, `Lib.Q.Value`, `Lib.PG.Q.Value`) at ≤ 0.01 controls the FDR at 1% among the identifications retained
- When match-between-runs is enabled, the library-level Q-values (`Lib.Q.Value`, `Lib.PG.Q.Value`) apply to the empirical library DIA-NN builds in its first pass, and we filter on them alongside the run-level Q-values
- `filterFeatures` applies row-level filters based on `rowData` variables, and can be applied to the whole `QFeatures` object or to specific sets
- Contaminant proteins (e.g., keratins, trypsin, BSA) should be removed before downstream analysis; including a curated contaminant database in the search and filtering on a `Cont_` prefix in `Protein.Ids` is a straightforward way to do this
- `joinAssays` combines per-sample `SummarizedExperiment` objects into a single combined set, with missing values (`NA`) where a precursor was not detected in a given sample
- `nNA` provides a convenient summary of missing values per feature (row) and per sample (column)
- DIA data typically has a relatively high proportion of missing values, as proteins must be detected independently in each sample
- The probability that a precursor is detected rises steadily with its intensity, with no fixed detection limit, so a missing value suggests low intensity but does not show that the precursor was absent
- We do not replace missing values; we filter sparse precursors, summarise proteins from observed precursors, and test only proteins quantified in enough samples of every group
- `filterNA` removes precursors that are missing above a specified proportion of samples, with the threshold chosen based on the experimental context
:::
